name: e-NatPOEM: Nature Photographs and Feelings
description:
How do nature photographs make people feel? This template rebuilds the rating procedure of the e-Nature Positive Emotions Photography Database (e-NatPOEM; Dal Fabbro, Catissi, Borba, Lima, Hingst-Zaher, Rosa, Victor, Oliveira, Souza & Leão 2021, Scientific Reports 11:11696). 739 Brazilian participants rated 433 photographs online (27,389 ratings). Most nature pictures were rated as pleasant and calming; their valence was higher and arousal lower than for control pictures in every category.

Participants first give age, gender, how often they are in contact with nature, education and monthly income. Photographs of water, landscapes and forests, pale and colourful birds, sky, flowers, insects and the sea then appear one at a time in random order, full screen for 9 s. Each is followed by two continuous Affective Sliders from 1 to 9 (valence: very unhappy to very happy; arousal: very relaxed to very excited; thumbs start in the middle and must be moved; slider order random on every picture). Participants also type one word for what the picture conveyed, then see a 5 s black screen. They rate as many pictures as they like and can press Finish at any time.

Data: affect (imageslidergroup, keyed by photo id) and feeling_word (custom, keyed by photo id: word, category, slider order, viewing and rating time). Analysis: mean valence and arousal per photograph and per category, plotted in the valence–arousal space; words grouped into themes.

Stimuli: the 395 nature photographs printed in Supplementary Material 2 of the paper, at the size published there (about 530 × 355 px), with the authors' photo ids. The photographers are co-authors João Rosa, Eliseth Ribeiro Leão, Luciano Lima, Erika Hingst-Zaher and Daniela Dal Fabbro. They are used here with credit to the authors and will be removed if the authors object.

Differences from the original study: (1) 395 of the 403 e-NatPOEM photographs (the ones printed in the supplement), at the supplement's resolution instead of 1600 × 1200; (2) the 28 control pictures (snakes, spiders, pollution) are not included, because the paper only describes them; (3) pictures come in a new random order for each participant instead of showing the least-rated picture first; (4) English wording instead of Portuguese, with emoji faces at the slider ends instead of the original Affective Slider icons; (5) categories are taken from the photo-id blocks of the supplement, and landscape and forest share one block.
author: Dal Fabbro et al.

elements.name: affect
elements.title: How did this picture make you feel?
elements.description: Affective Slider, continuous 1–9 (step 0.1), thumbs start in the middle and must be moved. valence: 1 = very unhappy … 9 = very happy; arousal: 1 = very relaxed … 9 = very excited. key = photo id (e.g. 042) as in Supplementary Material 2 of the paper. Each photograph is first shown full screen for 9 s.

elements.name: feeling_word
elements.title: In one word, what did the picture convey to you?
elements.description: One trial per photograph, key = photo id: { word, category, slider_order (valence_first | arousal_first) }. category follows the photo-id blocks of the paper's supplement: water 1–50, landscape_forest 51–100 and 406–448, pale_bird 101–150, colourful_bird 151–200, sky 201–250, flower 251–300, insect 301–350, sea 351–400; 479–480 (two birds of prey outside the numbered blocks) = bird_other.

config.description: Affective norms for nature photographs (e-NatPOEM). Photographs of water, landscapes and forests, pale and colourful birds, sky, flowers, insects and the sea are shown one at a time in random order, full screen for 9 s. Participants then rate how the picture made them feel on two continuous sliders from 1 to 9 (arousal: very relaxed to very excited; valence: very unhappy to very happy; slider order random on each picture), type one word for what the picture conveyed, and see a 5 s black screen before the next picture. They rate as many pictures as they like and can finish at any time. Rebuilt from Dal Fabbro et al. (2021), Scientific Reports, with the 395 photographs printed in the paper's Supplementary Material 2.
